articles.headline: OFAC Designates Guatemalan Narcotics and Terrorism Networks
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations on November 13, 2026, targeting counter narcotics and counter terrorism networks. The action specifically named 'LOS LORENZANAS' (also known as LORENZANA DRUG TRAFFICKING ORGANIZATION, 'THE LORENZANA CLAN', and 'THE LORENZANA FAMILY') in Guatemala.

This entity has been added to OFAC's Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) List and is identified as a Transnational Terrorist Group and a Criminal Organization. The designation carries secondary sanctions risk under section 1(b) of Executive Order 13224, as amended by Executive Order 13886.

This action underscores the U.S. government's ongoing efforts to disrupt international illicit drug trafficking and terrorist financing operations by targeting key organizations and their support networks.

articles.headline: OFAC Updates Iran-Related SDN List Entry for Volta Shipping Services
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued an Iran Designation Update on November 9, 2026, specifically modifying an existing entry on its Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) List. The update concerns Volta Shipping Services LLC, a UAE-based company.

The listed alias for Volta Shipping Services LLC has been changed from Volta Shipping Services FZCO to Volta Container Line FZCO. The company remains designated under Executive Order 13902 and continues to be subject to secondary sanctions risk.

This administrative update aims to ensure accuracy in OFAC's sanctions lists, reflecting changes in entity identification while maintaining the existing restrictive measures against the company due to its links to Mohammad Hossein Shamkhani and the Iranian economy.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / ABA Banking Journal

articles.headline: OFAC Sanctions Eight Canada-Based Money Services Businesses for Iran-Related Transactions
body: On November 6, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations, targeting eight Canada-based money services businesses. These entities are accused of operating in the digital asset sector of the Iranian economy, facilitating transactions involving Iran.

According to OFAC, these businesses exchange Iranian rials and other currencies for digital assets, and many have engaged with sanctioned Iranian cryptocurrency exchanges and digital asset addresses linked to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).

This action, coordinated with FinCEN and Canada's financial intelligence unit FINTRAC, was taken under Executive Order 13902, which targets key sectors of the Iranian economy. The designations aim to disrupt international financial channels used by Iran to evade sanctions.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / ABA Banking Journal / Federal Register

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Cuban and Chinese Entities, Expands Sanctions to Key Cuban Sectors
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced significant cyber-related and transnational criminal organization designations on November 5, 2026, alongside new Cuba designations and the publication of a Cuba-related determination. The U.S. designated Cuban oil shippers, Cuban state entities, and, for the first time, Chinese companies accused of supplying Cuba's military.

Specifically, OFAC extended Executive Order 14404 to include Cuba's manufacturing, technology, electronics, and marine sectors. This determination allows for future designations of foreign persons operating in these newly covered sectors.

Among the sanctioned Chinese entities are China National Electronics Import & Export Corporation (CEIEC) and Beijing H&C Technologies, a subsidiary of China Electronics Technology Group Corporation, both accused of supplying equipment to Cuba's military.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / World Socialist Web Site / CTV News

articles.headline: OFAC Issues New Iran-Related Designations and Amends Venezuela General License
body: On November 4, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations, updates to certain Iran-related listings, and the publication of an Iran-related OFAC Alert. Concurrently, OFAC issued an amended Venezuela-related General License and a Frequently Asked Question.

The Iran-related actions included sanctions against four individuals and nine entities allegedly linked to an India-based network supporting Iran's shadow fleet. OFAC also added a 'Secondary sanctions risk' notation to over 1,000 existing entries on the SDN List, primarily those designated under E.O. 13902, and to the Sectoral Sanctions Identifications List entry for VTB Bank.

Regarding Venezuela, OFAC issued General License 5AA, which authorizes transactions related to, financing for, and other dealings in the Petróleos de Venezuela, S.A. 2020 8.5 percent bond, effective December 18, 2026. This new general license replaces and supersedes General License 5Z.

body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued an amended Iran-related General License on October 29, 2026. This action modifies existing authorizations pertaining to transactions involving Iran.

While the specific details of the amendment were not immediately released, such changes typically aim to clarify, expand, or narrow the scope of permissible activities under the Iranian Transactions and Sanctions Regulations (ITSR).
Businesses and individuals engaging in Iran-related activities are advised to review the updated General License to ensure ongoing compliance with U.S. sanctions policy.

articles.region: North Korea, Democratic Republic of the Congo
articles.headline: OFAC Announces North Korea and DRC-Related Designations
body: On October 28, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations related to North Korea and the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). These actions target individuals and entities deemed to be involved in activities that undermine U.S. national security and foreign policy interests.

The North Korea designations are part of ongoing efforts to disrupt illicit revenue streams supporting the DPRK government, including those generated through overseas workers and malicious cyber activities.

The Democratic Republic of the Congo-related designations aim to address destabilizing activities within the region, often linked to armed groups and illicit resource exploitation. Further details on the specific individuals and entities designated were not immediately available in the initial announcement.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends FAQs on Blocking and Rejecting Transactions
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued amended Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) on October 26, 2026, regarding blocking and rejecting transactions and filing reports with OFAC. These updates aim to provide clearer guidance to financial institutions and other U.S. persons on their compliance obligations.

The amendments likely address common questions and provide updated interpretations or procedures for handling transactions involving sanctioned parties or jurisdictions. This includes guidance on when to block (freeze) funds or reject transactions, and the proper reporting mechanisms to OFAC.
Compliance professionals are encouraged to review the updated FAQs to ensure their internal procedures align with the latest OFAC guidance, thereby mitigating the risk of sanctions violations.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues New Iran, Russia General Licenses; Removes Belarus and North Korea Designations
body: On October 21, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations, alongside significant actions concerning Belarus and North Korea. OFAC also issued new Iran-related and Russia-related General Licenses and amended Frequently Asked Questions.

Notably, the announcement included the removal of certain designations related to Belarus and North Korea. These removals could signify a shift in policy or a determination that the conditions for their designation are no longer met.

The issuance of new General Licenses for Iran and Russia indicates specific authorizations for certain transactions that would otherwise be prohibited, aiming to facilitate particular activities while maintaining broader sanctions regimes. Amended FAQs provide further clarity on these complex sanctions programs.

articles.headline: EU Imposes New Sanctions on 113 Russian Individuals and Entities Over Ukraine War
body: The Council of the European Union announced on November 16, 2026, new restrictive measures against 12 individuals and 101 entities in response to Russia's ongoing war of aggression against Ukraine. These designations target economic sectors that provide substantial revenue to Russia's war effort and support its 'shadow fleet'.

The latest package includes nearly 50 Russian banks and financial institutions, aiming to further cut off financial channels funding the war. Also targeted are entities and businesspersons in the Russian oil and energy sector, including those managing Russian refineries and the St. Petersburg oil terminal.

The sanctions also extend to Russia's e-commerce giants, such as Ozon Bank LLC, Yandex Bank JSC, and Wildberries Bank, and individuals controlling significant stakes in these companies. Additionally, companies from the UAE, China, Seychelles, and Oman involved in buying Russian crude oil products and supporting Russia's shadow fleet have been listed.
articles.source: Council of the European Union / Morgan Lewis / EU NEIGHBOURS east

articles.headline: EU Sanctions 30 Individuals and Two Entities for Russian Cyber and Information Manipulation Activities
body: On November 16, 2026, the Council of the European Union decided to impose sanctions on 30 individuals and two entities for their involvement in Russia's malicious cyber activities and foreign information manipulation and interference (FIMI).

Among the sanctioned entities is the Social Design Agency (SDA), a Moscow-based public relations and political technology company accused of orchestrating large-scale information manipulation projects funded and supervised by the Russian Presidential Administration. The pro-Russian hacker group NoName057(16) was also listed for cyber-attacks on critical infrastructure in Ukraine, the U.S., and EU member states.

These restrictive measures include an asset freeze and travel bans for the individuals, prohibiting them from entering or transiting through EU member states. EU citizens and companies are also forbidden from making funds or economic resources available to those listed.
articles.source: Council of the European Union / EU NEIGHBOURS east / Eunews

articles.headline: UK Updates Sanctions List for Mansudae Overseas Project Group of Companies
body: On November 17, 2026, the UK's Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office updated the UK Sanctions List, specifically varying the entry for Mansudae Overseas Project Group of Companies under The Democratic People's Republic of Korea (Sanctions) (EU Exit) Regulations 2019.

The update includes additional information regarding the company's activities, noting its engagement in, facilitation of, or responsibility for the exportation of workers from the DPRK to other nations for construction-related activities, including for statues and monuments, to generate revenue for the Government of the DPRK or the Workers' Party of Korea.

Mansudae Overseas Project Group of Companies has been reported to conduct business in various countries in Africa and Southeast Asia. The sanctions imposed include an asset freeze, chartering of ships, closure of representative offices, crew servicing of ships and aircraft, prevention of business arrangements, and prohibition of port entry.

body: On November 16, 2026, the UN Security Council 1718 Sanctions Committee updated one entry on its sanctions list concerning the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK). The update pertains to the Mansudae Overseas Project Group of Companies.

The entry now includes additional information, noting that Mansudae Overseas Project Group of Companies has been involved in exporting workers from the DPRK to other nations for construction activities, including statues and monuments, to generate revenue for the DPRK government or the Workers' Party of Korea.
This amendment reflects ongoing international efforts to monitor and address activities that violate UN Security Council resolutions aimed at curbing North Korea's illicit revenue streams.

articles.headline: Ukraine Critically Damages Kerch Bridge, Intensifying Attacks on Russian Infrastructure
body: Ukraine has critically damaged the Kerch Bridge, which links occupied Crimea with Russia, following a series of drone and missile attacks. Footage showed a Ukrainian Flamingo cruise missile striking the road and railway crossing, causing an explosion and the collapse of an arch and a span of the bridge's road section.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky described the attack as a 'response to Russian strikes on our infrastructure,' indicating a long and complex campaign to demolish the bridge. Domestically produced drones, including Palianytsia, and Neptune missiles were reportedly used in the assault.

This latest strike follows an earlier attack on Monday and will force Moscow to 'completely overhaul' its supply routes to Crimea, shifting more traffic to the Novorossiya highway. Train travel across the bridge resumed briefly after the attack, but the railway line's arch was damaged.

articles.headline: BIS Imposes New Export Controls on Advanced AI Chips and Remote Access
body: On November 16, 2026, the U.S. Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced an interim final rule, 'Addressing Remote Access to Advanced Semiconductors,' which will go into effect on November 19.

The new rule introduces a data center end-use control, requiring a license to export, re-export, or transfer advanced chips and servers if the exporter knows the item is destined for a data center providing access to more than 12 million 'aggregate TPP' to companies headquartered in China, Country Group D:5 destinations (including Belarus and Russia), or Macau.

Additionally, a license will now be required for advanced computing items to or within Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil, due to their classification as countries with a 'higher-than-normal risk of diversion.' The rule also formally rescinds the Biden-era AI Diffusion Rule.
articles.source: U.S. Department of Commerce BIS / Mothership.SG / Reed Smith LLP

articles.headline: BIS 'Affiliates Rule' to Take Effect, Expanding Export Control Restrictions
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) 'Affiliates Rule' is set to take effect on November 10, 2026, expanding export control restrictions under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to companies owned or controlled by parties on certain restricted party lists.

This rule updates the EAR to prohibit export trade with companies that are directly or indirectly owned or controlled by parties on the BIS Entity List and its Military End User List. It harmonizes BIS ownership and control restrictions with OFAC's '50% Rule'.

The implementation of this rule will increase compliance obligations and enforcement risk for companies with international operations, particularly those with sourcing, distribution, or customer connections involving China. Companies are advised to review screening procedures and update trade compliance programs.

articles.headline: Revisions to the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) revises the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing two addresses associated with Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. from the Entity List under the destination of China, People's Republic of (China). This determination follows the removal from the Entity List of Arrow China Electronics Trading Co., Ltd., and the removal of six aliases for Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. in November 2025.

articles.headline: Removal From the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing one entity from the Entity List under the destination of Turkey.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.
